question: How stable are deterministic-finite-automaton rules extracted from different recurrent architectures and random initializations, especially when the source network is not perfectly trained?

key_findings.claim: Hidden-state quantization yields much smaller and more seed-stable automata than L*-style query extraction when the RNN oracle is imperfect.
key_findings.evidence: On partially trained Tomita models stopped after validation exceeds 85%, k-means and self-organizing-map extraction generally preserve usable accuracy, whereas L* fails on some LSTM/GRU Tomita-3 and Tomita-7 runs and produces highly variable state counts. On Tomita-5, L* outputs can exceed 200 states although the minimal target DFA has four; quantized outputs are usually below ten states.

anchors.section: Comparison of DFA extracted from Tomita Grammars and Partially Trained Tomita Grammars

key_findings.claim: Second-order RNNs produce the most reproducibly extractable symbolic dynamics in the tested architectures.
key_findings.evidence: Across ten initializations, O2RNN has 0% reported accuracy standard deviation on Tomita-6, versus 15.81% for LSTM, 23.85% for GRU, and 26.35% for MIRNN. Automata extracted from O2RNN are likewise described as having the best mean/variance tradeoff under partial training.

anchors.section: Performance of RNNs on Tomita Grammars

key_findings.claim: High neural recognition accuracy does not guarantee a stable or accurate finite-state explanation.
key_findings.evidence: LSTM and GRU reach near-perfect accuracy with fewer hidden units on bounded Dyck datasets, yet quantized O2RNN automata outperform their extracted automata across more state dimensions. Some L*-extracted LSTM/GRU automata fall below 50% while O2RNN extraction remains comparatively stable.

anchors.section: Dyck Languages, performance of RNNs and extracted DFAs

key_findings.claim: The empirical advantage of quantization grows on the paper's bounded Dyck tests, where query-derived machines vary strongly in both accuracy and size.
key_findings.evidence: The abstract reports 16%-22% accuracy deviations for L* with GRU/MIRNN versus 5%-15% for quantization, while O2RNN has 0.5%-3% deviations with either extractor. L* state counts can be on the order of 100, whereas quantization generally stays below 50.

anchors.section: Performance comparison of DFA extracted from Dyck Grammars

method.core_idea: Treat random initialization as a perturbation and compare the accuracy and size variability of finite-state rules extracted from first- and second-order recurrent networks.
method.mechanism: Train LSTM, GRU, O2RNN, and multiplicative-integration RNN classifiers on seven Tomita and four bounded Dyck datasets across ten seeds and several hidden sizes. Extract DFAs either by clustering hidden states with k-means/SOM, constructing observed transitions, majority-labeling accepting states, and minimizing, or by using the trained RNN as the membership/equivalence oracle for L*. Select the best of five quantized candidates on validation data and measure test accuracy and across-seed standard deviation/state count.
assumptions: Across-seed standard deviation of extracted-DFA test accuracy is an adequate operational definition of symbolic stability.
The synthetic string distributions and length bins adequately exercise the intended grammar rather than superficial frequency cues.
A DFA fitted on finite Dyck samples is a useful approximate explanation even though the unbounded language is not regular.
Validation selection among cluster counts is comparable to the single L* extraction procedure.
The approximate equivalence-query implementation supplies representative counterexamples to L*.
Differences among cell types are not dominated by architecture-specific optimization or parameter-count disparities.

techniques.role: Maps recurrent states to discrete DFA states and selects a compact validation-performing machine.
Provides a topology-aware alternative clustering discretization.
Actively constructs a candidate automaton through membership and approximate equivalence queries to the network.
Tests extraction before the neural oracle reaches perfect validation behavior.
Measures reproducibility in both predictive behavior and symbolic complexity.
Separates lengths 2-50 from a 51-100 test bin.

evaluations.setting: Seven Tomita regular languages, four recurrent cells, ten seeds, multiple hidden sizes
evaluations.metric: Network and extracted-DFA accuracy/standard deviation on lengths 2-50 and 51-100
evaluations.result: O2RNN and its extracted machines are generally most stable; on Tomita-6 O2RNN network accuracy has 0% seed deviation
evaluations.baseline: LSTM, GRU, MIRNN and both quantization- and L*-based extraction

evaluations.setting: Partially trained Tomita models stopped around 85%-90% validation accuracy
evaluations.metric: Extracted accuracy and number of states across seeds
evaluations.result: Quantized machines remain relatively compact/stable; L* sometimes fails and can exceed 100-200 states
evaluations.baseline: Perfectly trained models, where the two extractors have more similar accuracy

evaluations.metric: Accuracy and standard deviation of networks/DFAs across ten seeds
evaluations.result: GRU is often the best neural classifier, but quantized O2RNN machines are the most consistently accurate; L* sometimes falls below chance
evaluations.baseline: LSTM, GRU, MIRNN, O2RNN with L*, k-means, and SOM

evaluations.metric: Mode, minimum, and maximum extracted state count
evaluations.result: L* counts can reach hundreds and vary sharply; quantization is typically much smaller
evaluations.baseline: Known minimal Tomita DFA sizes and cross-seed mode

limitations: A finite automaton cannot recognize an unbounded Dyck language, so the Dyck results describe approximation on bounded sampled lengths, not extraction of the true context-free rule.
The paper's fixed-point stability definitions are not directly estimated; the experiments operationalize stability mainly as seed-wise accuracy deviation and state-count spread.
Quantization gets validation-based selection among five cluster-count candidates, while L* is sensitive to one counterexample process, creating an asymmetric comparison.

A compact quantized DFA may smooth away genuine rare RNN behavior and thus be less faithful even when it matches the target labels better; fidelity to the source network is not separated from task accuracy.
The abstract reports 3,600 networks/18,000 quantized DFAs plus 3,600 L* DFAs, while the methodology says 3,200/16,000/3,200, leaving the experimental count internally inconsistent.
Only ten seeds, synthetic binary grammars, accuracy, and descriptive deviations are used; there are no confidence intervals or hypothesis tests.
Architecture comparisons do not clearly match parameter count, training difficulty, or hyperparameter-search budget.
The approximate equivalence-query/counterexample procedure and its compute budget are insufficiently characterized for reproducibility.
failure_modes: L* chases inconsistent errors of an imperfect neural oracle and proliferates states rather than recovering the intended grammar.
Clustering merges distinct hidden regimes that are rare in the finite extraction corpus, producing a compact but unfaithful DFA.
Validation chooses a cluster count that overfits the sampled length range and fails on longer strings.
A bounded Dyck test rewards a finite-state shortcut that cannot maintain an unbounded stack.
Low across-seed variance masks consistent bias shared by every extracted machine.
reusable_insights: Evaluate symbolic explanations on reproducibility, compactness, target accuracy, and behavioral fidelity as separate axes.
Stress an extractor with partially trained and noisy source models rather than only perfectly separable benchmarks.
When an active learner assumes a consistent oracle, treat model errors as label noise or regularize automaton growth explicitly.
Do not infer that a network learned an unbounded formal rule from bounded-length accuracy or from a finite-state surrogate.
open_questions: Can noisy-oracle variants of active automata learning recover compact machines without overreacting to isolated RNN errors?
How should one measure the Pareto frontier between DFA compactness, fidelity to the RNN, target-language accuracy, and seed stability?
Do the O2RNN advantages persist under matched parameters and modern optimization on natural, multiclass, or probabilistic sequence tasks?
Can pushdown or weighted-automaton extraction represent context-free behavior more faithfully than bounded DFAs?

competitive_landscape.title: Extracting Automata from Recurrent Neural Networks Using Queries and Counterexamples
competitive_landscape.difference: Weiss et al. combine L* with abstraction to seek a DFA faithful to a trained RNN, emphasizing fine state distinctions; the reviewed paper focuses on cross-seed target accuracy/compactness and finds that imperfect oracles make this approach unstable.

competitive_landscape.title: Connecting Weighted Automata and Recurrent Neural Networks through Spectral Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: alternative formal bridge and learning method
competitive_landscape.difference: Rabusseau et al. prove equivalence between linear second-order RNNs and weighted finite automata and give a spectral recovery algorithm; the reviewed work studies nonlinear trained cells and hard DFA extraction empirically.

competitive_landscape.title: Sequential Neural Networks as Automata
competitive_landscape.difference: Merrill classifies recurrent architectures through asymptotic state complexity under finite precision; the reviewed paper tests whether discrete rules can be reproducibly recovered from gradient-trained instances.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Networks and the Chomsky Hierarchy
competitive_landscape.difference: Deletang et al. evaluate 20,910 models on 15 tasks and show structured memory is needed for context-free extrapolation; the reviewed paper narrows attention to DFA explanation stability and therefore cannot establish true Dyck recognition.

competitive_landscape.title: Thinking Like Transformers
competitive_landscape.relationship: competing symbolic abstraction for sequence models
competitive_landscape.difference: Weiss et al. specify a high-level RASP program model for Transformer computation rather than extracting a finite automaton from trajectories; it offers constructive explanations for tasks, while the reviewed methods are post-hoc and RNN-specific.

novelty_assessment: The valuable contribution is the cross-seed, partial-training comparison of compact quantization against query-based extraction across several recurrent cells. The conclusion that O2RNN plus quantization is stable is useful evidence, but it is narrower than the prose suggests: the stability metric is behavioral, the method comparison is asymmetric, experimental counts conflict, and bounded DFA fits to Dyck data cannot certify recovery of context-free structure.
reviewer_notes: Read all 17 extracted pages, including training grids and appendix figures. Primary arXiv records for query/counterexample extraction, spectral weighted-automata recovery, automata-based RNN capacity, the Chomsky-hierarchy benchmark, and RASP were checked on 2026-08-23. The 3,600-versus-3,200 model-count inconsistency and the finite-DFA limitation on Dyck languages were explicitly audited.
